title: Platform systems & services — dashboards, alerts, runbooks, roadmap, and retrospective
author: Aisha Patel
body:
Overview:

This page consolidates the Platform Engineering team’s living reference for systems and services inventory, dashboards and alerts, runbooks for common incidents, recent retrospective findings, and the near-term roadmap. It is intended for oncall engineers, SREs, and platform owners who operate Redwood’s internal platform systems and customer-facing services.

Goals:

- Reduce mean time to detection and resolution (MTTD/MTTR) for platform incidents.
- Maintain high signal/noise for alerts and keep actionable page counts below targets.
- Provide clear runbooks for the top 10 failure modes.
- Align the roadmap to reliability gaps identified in retrospectives.

Scope:

This document covers: core platform services (kafka-ingest, routing-proxy, model-scheduler), observability stacks, dashboards and SLOs, alerting rules, primary runbooks, and a 90-day roadmap plus retrospective actions. Private deployment packages and customer-specific runbooks live under eng-private-deployments.

Dashboards & Alerts:

Design principles:
- Dashboards show the SLOs, error budgets, and ten-minute retros: immediate context for oncall.
- Alerts only fire when human action is likely to change the outcome. Avoid informational noise.
- Use grouping and dependencies so follow-up alerts do not create duplicates.

Key dashboards (links internal):
- Routing Overview — latency, error rate by route, token throughput, backend saturation.
- Scheduler Health — queue lengths, retry rates, worker availability, slow jobs by model family.
- Cache Health — hit rates by keyspace, eviction churn, memory pressure, cold-starts.
- Ingest Pipeline — consumer lag, partition distribution, producer retry rates.
- Observability Health — scrape success, metrics latency, alerting pipeline throughput.

Alerting thresholds (examples):

1) routing-proxy_high_error_rate (pager):
- Condition: 5m error rate > 2% AND p99 latency > 1s
- Priority: P1
- Runbook: Routing proxy degraded — follow runbook steps below

2) model-scheduler_queue_growth (pager):
- Condition: queue depth grows 3x baseline for 10m OR backlog > 10k jobs
- Priority: P1
- Runbook: Scheduler backlog surge — scale actions + slow-path fallback

3) metrics-ingest_scrape_failure (slack):
- Condition: 10% scrape failure across >20% targets for 5m
- Priority: P2 (page if >50% targets oncall)

Alert management best practices:
- All alerts must include a clear owner, symptom, and first-step mitigation.
- Use silence windows for planned maintenance; automate via the incident platform.
- Quarterly review of alert efficacy; retire alerts with >50% false positive rate.

Runbooks (top-level):

A. Routing proxy degraded (P1) — first 15 minutes
1. Check routing-proxy dashboard: error rate, p95/p99 latency, backend availability.
2. If error rate spike: run `kubectl -n infra get pods -lapp=routing-proxy -o wide` to inspect restarts.
3. Look at downstream backends: are model-serving pods healthy? Follow backend-specific runbook.
4. If CPU throttling or host OOMs present, scale up routing-proxy replicas and open a host capacity ticket.
5. If caused by a bad rollout, rollback the deployment: `kubectl -n infra rollout undo deploy/routing-proxy` and monitor.
6. If routing traffic needs to be shed, flip route fallback to canary model-variant (see traffic-fallback runbook).

B. Scheduler backlog surge (P1) — first 30 minutes
1. Identify the offending job type and model family in Scheduler Health dashboard.
2. Increase worker pool size (k8s HPA) or provision a burst pool via dedicated-capacity job queue.
3. If backlog persists, enable slow-path (best-effort batching) to preserve latency SLOs for critical routes.
4. Notify customer-facing teams if SLA impact expected.

C. Cache cold-start / low hit-rate (P2)
1. Inspect KV cache hit-rate by keyspace. Run cache warmup for inactive keyspaces if necessary.
2. Check eviction churn and memory pressure; increase cache memory or adjust TTLs.
3. If due to recent restart, coordinate with deploy owner to stagger restarts.

Oncall escalation matrix:

- 0–15m: oncall engineer performs runbook actions
- 15–45m: oncall requests platform-ic if remediation needs cross-team coordination
- 45m+: incident declared, incident commander engaged, postmortem templated

Procedures & How-tos (short):

- Add a new dashboard:
  1. Create a Grafana dashboard with SLO panels and an errors/traffic panel.
  2. Add dashboard to ownership file (engineering/obs/dashboards.yaml).
  3. Add alert rules in Prometheus/ruler with clear runbook links.
  4. Submit for review to Observability Team and include test query screenshots.

- Update an alert threshold:
  1. Triage recent alert history for false positives.
  2. Propose a threshold change in PR with annotated test ranges.
  3. Run a 2-week A/B test with reduced sensitivity in a staging namespace.

Operational Metrics & Targets:

- Mean time to detect (MTTD): target < 2 minutes for P1 alerts
- Mean time to resolution (MTTR): target < 30 minutes for P1 incidents
- Alert noise: actionable alerts per week per oncall < 5
- Dashboard coverage: 100% of platform-critical services have SLO dashboards

90-day Roadmap (high level):

Q1 initiatives (next 90 days):
- Reduce routing-proxy p99 by 20ms via kernel tuning and HTTP/2 keepalive adjustments (owner: infra perf)
- Implement automated alert suppression for known cascade patterns (owner: observability)
- Expand cache warmup tooling to support pre-warming on deploys (owner: platform services)
- Add churn detection to metrics-ingest to reduce false-positive scrape failures (owner: observability)

Planned improvements beyond 90 days:
- Centralize runbook execution steps in the incident platform for one-click mitigation actions
- Introduce model-variant traffic shaping to reduce tail latency in routing-proxy

Recent retrospective (last incident review):

Incident: routing-proxy partial outage, 2026-01-21
Summary:
- Root cause: a combination of an upstream mesh proxy regression and an aggressive routing-proxy CPU limit causing request queuing and increased p99 latency.
- Impact: brief (~12m) elevated latency affecting ~8% of requests; no data loss.

Key findings and action items:
1. CPU limits were too aggressive for the new proxy version. Action: increase default CPU request to 500m for routing-proxy; PR merged (owner: infra).
2. Mesh proxy upgrades should require a canary with traffic shaping. Action: update deployment gating checklist (owner: release-engineering).
3. Alerting gap: p95 latency alone did not trigger a page; add combined error-rate + p99 rule (owner: observability).
4. Post-incident follow-up: schedule a game-day to validate rollbacks and scale procedures (owner: platform-sre).

Retrospective status tracker:
- CPU request change: done
- Canary gating update: in_progress (expected complete 2026-02-20)
- Alert rule update: done
- Game-day: scheduled 2026-03-05

Appendix: Example Prometheus alert rule (illustrative)

ALERT routing_proxy_degraded
  IF (sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="routing-proxy",status!~"2.."}[5m])) by (instance) / sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="routing-proxy"}[5m])) by (instance)) > 0.02
  AND histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{job="routing-proxy"}[5m])) by (le)) > 1
  FOR 5m
  LABELS { severity="page" }
  ANNOTATIONS { summary="High error rate and elevated p99 on routing-proxy", runbook="/confluence/eng-platform/platform-systems-services-runbook-2026-q1#routing-proxy" }

Notes:
- This page is a living document; keep it concise and actionable.
- Major changes to dashboards or alerts should include a short migration plan and owner sign-off.
